opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there are a few reasons, and they all come back to what our customers actually care about.

First is control. When you're an enterprise, your data is your most valuable asset, and many of our customers are understandably nervous about sending that data outside their environment to a third-party API. With an open model, they can run it inside their own infrastructure and their own security perimeter, and they know exactly where the data goes. For regulated industries like finance, healthcare, and government, that's often not optional. It's a requirement.

Second is customization. Very few enterprises will get the most value from a generic model used as-is. The real value comes when you take a strong base model and adapt it to your domain, your terminology, your tasks, by fine-tuning or continued pretraining on your own data. You can only do that in a deep way if you have the weights. And once you've done it, that customized model becomes a piece of intellectual property for the company, something that differentiates them, rather than something they rent.

Third is cost and efficiency. DBRX used a mixture-of-experts architecture, so only a fraction of the parameters are active for any given token. That gives you good quality at much better inference cost and latency. For enterprises running these models at scale, the economics really matter, and owning the model lets them optimize serving for their own workloads.

And finally, there's a broader point. We've always believed in open source at Databricks. With Spark, Delta Lake, MLflow, we saw that open ecosystems move faster, attract more innovation, and give customers confidence that they're not locked in. We wanted to show that you don't have to depend on a handful of closed providers to get a high-quality model. You can build one, and maybe more importantly, we wanted to show customers that the tools and the know-how exist for them to build or adapt their own. DBRX was partly a demonstration of that: here's what's possible with the platform, and you can do it too.

So for us, it wasn't just about releasing a model. It was about giving enterprises ownership over their AI, the same way they want ownership over their data.

r001.rationale: The response discusses keeping data inside an enterprise’s security perimeter, but does not say that decisions can be traced back to the data used to make them.

r002.rationale: It says enterprises can run the open model inside their own infrastructure and security perimeter.

r003.rationale: It describes DBRX as a strong base model that enterprises can fine-tune on their own data for their domain and tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it comes back to what we've believed since the very beginning of Databricks, which is that the real value for an enterprise is in its own data. So if you think about where the enterprise is going with AI, they don't just want a general-purpose model that knows a little bit about everything. They want a model that understands their business, their documents, their customers, their domain. And to get there, you need to be able to customize the model, to fine-tune it, to do retrieval on top of it, and ultimately to own it.

With a closed model behind an API, you can't really do that. You're sending your data to someone else, you don't control the weights, you don't control the roadmap, and you don't control the cost. And for many enterprises, especially in regulated industries, that's just not acceptable. They have concerns about privacy, about governance, about lock-in.

So when we released DBRX, the point wasn't just to show that we could train a frontier-quality open model, although I think that was important, because it showed that you don't need to be one of two or three labs in the world to do this. The point was to demonstrate to our customers that this entire path is available to them. The data pipelines, the training infrastructure, the evaluation, the serving, all of it on their data, on the platform they already use. DBRX was in some sense the proof that the recipe works.

And there's a broader thing too. Open models move the whole field faster. People can study them, build on them, find the problems. We benefited enormously from the open-source ecosystem, with Spark, with Ray, with everything that came out of the Berkeley labs. So it felt very natural to contribute back in the same way. I think in the long run, the best models for most enterprises will be the ones they can actually control, and open weights are the foundation for that.

r001.rationale: The response mentions privacy, governance, and control, but does not identify tracing decisions back to the data used to make them as an auditability need.

r002.rationale: It says the DBRX recipe can run on customers’ data and the platform they already use, but does not clearly say enterprises can host the model within infrastructure they control.

r003.rationale: It says enterprises need to customize and fine-tune models to understand their business, and presents DBRX as demonstrating a path customers can use on their own data.

astra-6.text:
For enterprise customers, a big concern is control. They have proprietary data, and they want to use that data to build models that are useful for their business without giving up control over it. With an open model, they can run it in their own environment, understand what they’re deploying, and customize it for their needs.

We saw DBRX as a way to give customers that choice. They can use a capable model directly, or use it as a starting point and fine-tune it with their own data. And they’re not locked into a single provider. Ultimately, the value for an enterprise is in combining the model with its own data and applications, and openness gives them more flexibility to do that.

r001.rationale: The response discusses control over proprietary data, but does not say enterprises need to trace decisions back to the data used to make them.

r002.rationale: It says customers can run the open model in their own environment, communicating that they can host it within infrastructure they control.

r003.rationale: It describes DBRX as a starting point customers can fine-tune with their own data for their needs.

sol-6.1.text:
For enterprise customers, a lot of the value comes from combining a model with their own data. They want control over that data, control over where the model runs, and the ability to customize it for their applications. With an open model, they can do that without depending entirely on a single provider.

Releasing DBRX was also a way to show what’s possible and give customers a strong starting point. They can evaluate it, adapt it, and make their own tradeoffs around quality, cost, and latency. We think that choice is very important.

r001.rationale: The response discusses customer control and choice, but does not identify tracing decisions back to the data used as an auditability need.

r002.rationale: It says customers want control over where the model runs, which communicates the ability to host it within infrastructure they control.

r003.rationale: It calls DBRX a strong starting point and mentions adapting and customizing it, but does not clearly say customers fine-tune it with their own data for specific use cases.
